article.title: Universities Are Teaching the Virtue of Overwork
article.author: Nicholas Liu
article.content: Although the University of Chicago bears “Let knowledge grow from more to more; and so be human life enriched” as its official motto, a different slogan entirely has attained much wider fame. Thanks to long-cemented campus lore, the university is best known instead by the refrain of its student body: “Where fun goes to die.” The slogan is spoken in weary, ironic tones, suggesting a strange marriage of acceptance and self-congratulation. Yes, life can be miserable, and yes, the vigor of UChicago’s curriculum is exactly what I came here for, and it will not break me . Stanford University and the University of Pennsylvania (Penn) have their own versions — “ Duck syndrome ” and “ Penn Face ,” respectively — the brave demeanor a student puts on to hide their stress. To suffer is a mark of virtue, and there is a perverse sense of pride that bleeds out of it — if a student is not suffering, do they truly belong at their institution? Imani Wade, a college student beginning her fourth year at UChicago, told Jacobin that mutual misery seemed to be the point. “There was this kind of bonding over the fact that we’re all in the study room until 3 a.m., and we’re all sporadically crying at different moments, and then we all have 9:30s and 8:30s the next day that we’re going to still go to,” she said. “Even now, in my third and fourth year, I feel like there’s never a time when I should not have anything to do.” Wade’s description of student life as a mirror of the modern American workplace captures a transformation of colleges over the last half-century, from institutions nominally dedicated to civic and intellectual development to what scholar and cultural critic Henry Giroux, in an interview with Jacobin , called “little more than an adjunct of corporate efficiency [and] corporate logic.” This transformation is visible in the hollowing-out of humanities departments, the reduction of faculty to precarious adjunct labor , and the punitive suppression of student unions. But the structural conditioning of students to accept their own exploitation — and if they are successful, the subsequent management of others — remains the modern university’s most profound ideological victory. “Many students are pressured to define themselves in terms of how the university is going to reward them,” Giroux said. “This kind of culture says you must overwork, it says you must overperform, it says you must beat everybody else out, it says that you must organize yourself around the values of the market, competition, productivity, efficiency, and conformity.” Deep-seated American cultural beliefs equating ceaseless toil with divine grace predate the founding of the country itself, serving as a convenient framework for justifying chattel slavery or framing unionizing workers as lazy and ungrateful. With the expansion of the white-collar managerial class, the university has become a primary site for this cultural reproduction. While the apparently Calvinist-flavored ethos generally takes on a less overtly religious character on college campuses, the underlying theology remains the same: work is not only a practical means for professional advancement but a virtue in and of itself. All-nighters, skipped meals, and stress-induced panic take on the character of redemptive sacrifice, while having nothing to do while colleagues toil constitutes a moral failing . This shows up in “a big culture of busy-bragging that is really endemic to a lot of workplace cultures in the United States, where people feel like they have to prove that they belong through talking about how overwhelmed that they are all of the time,” Devon Price, a social psychologist, told Jacobin . “If you’re going to try and really belong in those spaces, it is all about putting forward this front or living that reality that you are just sacrificing your life for your career.” To their credit, college administrations have generally avoided “fun goes to die”–style slogans in favor of more sanitized narratives. Marquette University’s installation of high-tech “ nap pods ” in libraries, pitched as a “wellness” initiative, baits students into staying in the library rather than going home to rest on their own beds. That logic — sleep as recharge for work rather than a fundamental human need — is the same logic Amazon uses when installing “mindfulness chambers” on its warehouse floors. Institutions like Johns Hopkins University and the University of Southern California , meanwhile, have partnered with corporate meditation apps like Calm and Headspace to provide free subscriptions for their students. Penn’s administration, not to be outdone, runs a “ Resilience Program ,” available by online request, that trains students to “thrive in challenging environments” and “overcome counter-productive thinking habits that undercut performance.” What these universities don’t seem to relinquish to their students is the actual workload they assign. Wade told Jacobin that in her first year, she would have to stay up until 2 a.m. or 3 a.m. three times a week. “I was in the college for only about a month and a half before my birthday came around, and I physically broke down on my birthday, and I didn’t want to do anything, and I vividly remember that being one of the worst birthdays I’ve had, just because of the stress, and I was not sleeping well,” she said. Misery, then, is framed not as a structural failure of universities that overwork their students but as a personal failing of students who lack the fortitude to, in Penn’s own vocabulary, thrive in challenging environments and overcome counterproductive thinking habits that undercut performance. But all of it is justified in the end. A student who is smart or hardworking or rich enough to attend an elite university makes a calculated wager: they choose to submit to a crucible that promises to train them for the professional or intellectual vanguard, accepting whatever pains come with it. To Endure Is a Virtue Universities did not invent the labor market that punishes workers for refusing to absorb its costs, but they are among its most useful enablers. Their reputations depend on where their graduates land, and their donors are often the firms doing the hiring, so the message they send students never varies: there is no alternative to accepting their own exploitation. When graduate and undergraduate student workers attempt to unionize, administrations routinely spend millions of dollars on hiring corporate antiunion lawyers, asserting before the National Labor Relations Board that collective bargaining defiles the sacred educational relationship between university and student. Rather than passively preparing and releasing students into the labor market, they invite elite financial and consulting firms to dictate campus culture and legitimize their dominance through aggressive recruiting and networking events where students get to taste the elite and hallowed space that may one day be theirs. A university degree has become both an academic achievement and a message to employers: this worker will accept an eighty-hour workweek, endure immense psychological pressure, and pass the tradition on to the students who come after. Recognizing the precariousness of the modern capitalist economy, students willingly participate in the credentialing process, viewing their own endurance as a rational sacrifice. “How is it that students can work themselves to death and not be critically reflective about how it undermines their sense of agency?” Giroux asked. The answer, he said, is that the university leaves them with neither the energy nor mental space to recognize it. “Students have to fight for grants, they are graded on a curve where their success is based on everyone else’s performance . . . all that entails an obligation to, in some way, uphold these kinds of values that increasingly resemble a sorting machine,” he said. “When you organize the university around discipline, competitiveness, and market values, the solidarity and democratic culture disappears, and it is difficult to imagine yourself in a role outside of having to get out of there, and if you have to kill yourself and end up being therapeutically damaged for years, that’s the price you pay.” Predictably, those practices, ostensibly designed to prepare students for the workforce, end up sabotaging them. Elite colleges frame impossible volumes of coursework as a character-building exercise that makes students smarter than everyone else — the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, for example, glibly likens it to “drinking from a firehose.” Much as a high-velocity column of water will instantly shatter a drinker’s internal organs, this kind of coursework usually ends up biologically short-circuiting the brain and ensuring the material is rapidly forgotten, if retained at all. “Overwork really hasn’t really helped me actually understand any of the things I was supposed to be understanding,” Wade said. The grading curve, meanwhile, enforces hostile competition among students, rather than measuring them against the material they are supposed to be learning. Because it relies on artificial scarcity — condemning a predetermined number of students to a low grade regardless of objective mastery — collaboration is structurally punished. The result of this “peer-status competition,” according to two major research studies , has been to drive students away from their chosen disciplines, particularly in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), where introductory “weed-out” courses explicitly designed to fail massive percentages of the student body are especially common. Most of the victims are, naturally, low-income and first-generation students who lack years of private tutoring to arm themselves and a generational safety net to absorb the shock. Hard sciences and the humanities, two fields that look less overtly professional than finance or law, fall under the same exploitative logic. “The life of the mind” is a convenient way to obscure the fact that being a scientist now usually means providing cheap labor for an institution that channels their research into private profit, rather than harnessing it for the public good; after all, the rationale goes, if scientists truly cared about curing a disease, their working conditions should be trivial. Meanwhile, those in the humanities, increasingly starved of grants and graduate school space by systemic budget cuts, find their own intellectual curiosity turned into a competitive commodity and noble pursuit for which they might willingly sacrifice their own material dignity. The overwork-for-credentials bargain is losing legitimacy. Two decades of financial crashes, wage stagnation, and a graduate labor market that absorbs fewer of the people credentialed for it have stripped the promise of its plausibility. “Hard work” was always a thin veneer for exploitation, but even the material scraps that people have been driven by desperation to accept are now out of reach. Younger people especially are unmoved by the narratives that have long upheld the capitalist labor market, simply because the math no longer adds up. “I think they’re more depressed than they are overloaded with stress, which is already a pretty big change from a couple of years ago,” Price said. “As the system fractures, people are seeing what a lie this set of beliefs always was. What we’re going to actually do about it certainly remains an open question, but it does seem like the wheels are kind of coming off the machine.”
